777fae40-2377-5e63-89f6-5c857beba2b2.title: Classifying an Isolated Critical Point of a Nonlinear System

e-21675.problem:
Given the system of differential equations, determine whether the system is almost linear at the equilibrium point $\mathbf{x}^\ast= [0, \: 0]^T.$

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t)=-{y}^{2}(t)+1-{e}^{x(t)} \\ {y}^{′}(t)=-{x}^{2}(t)+1-{e}^{y(t)}\end{aligned}
$$
e-21675.worked_solution:
The system can be rewritten in matrix form as 

$$
\mathbf{x}' = \boldsymbol{f}(\mathbf{x})
$$

where ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14094758/assets/58d027aeb94fddf42231a86a73de4be306fa6ea22ea7767dbe8a461e91a6f446.png) and 
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14094758/assets/bb9297479f2149dfca76e02fb9e314205063fd3a3f967d70eee24235970206b1.png)

We need to compute the Jacobian determinant of $\boldsymbol{f}(\mathbf{x}).$ 

In our case, we have the following:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14094758/assets/6ea02cc0d71b67f061adb67ee344cc5474b71e1e34db122b942d2e0ed1531ae8.png)

First, we compute the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(-{y}^{2}+1-{e}^{x})=-{e}^{x},\, & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(-{y}^{2}+1-{e}^{x})=-2y \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(-{x}^{2}+1-{e}^{y})=-2x,\, & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(-{x}^{2}+1-{e}^{y})=-{e}^{y}\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, we have

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14094758/assets/8f1e68dd09715b24f0de6c79fdf07af6e9810741e1a6065637db5301cd86ebe0.png)

Next, we evaluate the Jacobian at the equilibrium ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14094758/assets/ef4a060144a80ac9ecb94a71c407d1537283ecc217ac26ab053e9b8d2fad73e9.png) to get

$$
\begin{aligned}J(0,0) & =|\begin{aligned}-{e}^{0} & -2(0) \\ -2(0) & -{e}^{0}\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}-1 & 0 \\ 0 & -1\end{aligned}| \\  & =(-1)(-1)-(0)(0) \\  & =1 \\  & \ne 0.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, since the Jacobian determinant is not zero, our system is $\bbox[4pt, border: solid 1pt gainsboro]{\text{almost linear}}$ at $\mathbf{x}^\ast.$

$$

Consider the system of differential equations above. What is the corresponding linearized system at the equilibrium point $\mathbf{x}^\ast=[2, \ 0]^T?$
e-21674.worked_solution:
The system can be rewritten in matrix form as 

$$
\mathbf{x}' = \boldsymbol{f}(\mathbf{x})

decision.explanation: The Jacobian matrix is [[sin(πy), πx cos(πy)], [−π sin(πx), 2y]]. At (0,0), every entry is zero, so its determinant is zero. By the lesson's criterion, the system is not almost linear at this equilibrium.

after.name: Question 1
after.problem:
$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t)=x(t)\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi y(t)) \\ {y}^{′}(t)={y}^{2}(t)+\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi x(t))-1\end{aligned}
$$

Given the system of differential equations, select the correct options below.The Jacobian determinant of the system at the equilibrium point ${x}^{∗}=[0,\text{ }0]^{T}$ is given as

$$
J(0,0)={{field-1}}.
$$

At this point, the system is 
{{field-2}}
at ${x}^{∗}.$
after.worked_solution:
The system can be rewritten in matrix form as 

$$
{x}^{′}=f(x)
$$

where $x=[\begin{aligned}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{aligned}]$ and 
$f(x)=[\begin{aligned}x\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi y) \\ {y}^{2}+\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi x)-1\end{aligned}].$

We need to compute the Jacobian determinant of $f(x).$ 

In our case, we have the following:

$$
J=|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂x} & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂y} \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂x} & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂y}\end{aligned}|
$$

First, we compute the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(x\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi y))=\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi y),\, & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(x\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi y))=\pi x\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi y) \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({y}^{2}+\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi x)-1)=-\pi \operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi x),\, & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({y}^{2}+\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi x)-1)=2y\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, we have

$$
J=|\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi y) & \pi x\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi y) \\ -\pi \operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi x) & 2y\end{aligned}|.
$$

Next, we evaluate the Jacobian at the equilibrium ${x}^{∗}=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0\end{aligned}]$ to get

$$
\begin{aligned}J(0,0) & =|\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡(0) & \pi (0)\operatorname{cos}⁡(0) \\ -\pi \operatorname{sin}⁡(0) & 2(0)\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}| \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, since the Jacobian determinant is zero, our system is $\text{not almost linear}$ at ${x}^{∗}.$

EXPLANATION

The system can be rewritten in matrix form as x′=f(x) where x=[x(t)y(t)] and f(x)=[xsin⁡(πy)y2+cos⁡(πx)−1].

We need to compute the Jacobian determinant of f(x).

In our case, we have the following:

J=|∂f1∂x∂f1∂y∂f2∂x∂f2∂y|

First, we compute the partial derivatives:

∂f1∂x=∂∂x(xsin⁡(πy))=sin⁡(πy),∂f1∂y=∂∂y(xsin⁡(πy))=πxcos⁡(πy)∂f2∂x=∂∂x(y2+cos⁡(πx)−1)=−πsin⁡(πx),∂f2∂y=∂∂x(y2+cos⁡(πx)−1)=2y

Thus, we have

J=|sin⁡(πy)πxcos⁡(πy)−πsin⁡(πx)2y|.

Next, we evaluate the Jacobian at the equilibrium x∗=[00] to get

J(0,0)=|sin⁡(0)π(0)cos⁡(0)−πsin⁡(0)2(0)|=|0000|=0.

Finally, since the Jacobian determinant is zero, our system is not almost linear at x∗.

content.worked_solution:
The system can be rewritten in matrix form as 

$$
{x}^{′}=\text{\boldsymbol}f(x)
$$

where $x=[\begin{aligned}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{aligned}]$ and 
$\text{\boldsymbol}f(x)=[\begin{aligned}x\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi y) \\ {y}^{2}+\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi x)-1\end{aligned}].$

We need to compute the Jacobian determinant of $\text{\boldsymbol}f(x).$ 

In our case, we have the following:

$$
J=|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂x} & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂y} \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂x} & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂y}\end{aligned}|
$$

First, we compute the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(x\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi y))=\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi y),\, & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(x\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi y))=\pi x\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi y) \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({y}^{2}+\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi x)-1)=-\pi \operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi x),\, & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({y}^{2}+\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi x)-1)=2y\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, we have

$$
J=|\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi y) & \pi x\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi y) \\ -\pi \operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi x) & 2y\end{aligned}|.
$$

Next, we evaluate the Jacobian at the equilibrium ${x}^{∗}=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0\end{aligned}]$ to get

$$
\begin{aligned}J(0,0) & =|\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡(0) & \pi (0)\operatorname{cos}⁡(0) \\ -\pi \operatorname{sin}⁡(0) & 2(0)\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}| \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, since the Jacobian determinant is zero, our system is $\text{not almost linear}$ at ${x}^{∗}.$

after.problem:
$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t)={y}^{2}(t)+\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi x(t)) \\ {y}^{′}(t)={x}^{2}(t)+\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi y(t))\end{aligned}
$$

Given the system of differential equations, select the correct options below.The Jacobian determinant of the system at the equilibrium point ${x}^{∗}=[1,\text{ }1]^{T}$ is given as

$$
J(1,1)={{field-1}}.
$$

At this point, the system is 
{{field-2}}
at ${x}^{∗}.$
after.worked_solution:
The system can be rewritten in matrix form as 

$$
{x}^{′}=f(x)
$$

where $x=[\begin{aligned}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{aligned}]$ and 
$f(x)=[\begin{aligned}{y}^{2}+\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi x) \\ {x}^{2}+\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi y)\end{aligned}].$

We need to compute the Jacobian determinant of $f(x).$ 

In our case, we have the following:

$$
J=|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂x} & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂y} \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂x} & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂y}\end{aligned}|
$$

First, we compute the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({y}^{2}+\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi x))=-\pi \operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi x),\, & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({y}^{2}+\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi x))=2y \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}+\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi y))=2x,\, & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}+\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi y))=-\pi \operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi y)\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, we have

$$
J=|\begin{aligned}-\pi \operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi x) & 2y \\ 2x & -\pi \operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi y)\end{aligned}|.
$$

Next, we evaluate the Jacobian at the equilibrium ${x}^{∗}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]$ to get

$$
\begin{aligned}J(1,1) & =|\begin{aligned}-\pi \operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi (1)) & 2(1) \\ 2(1) & -\pi \operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi (1))\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}0 & 2 \\ 2 & 0\end{aligned}| \\  & =0\cdot 0-2\cdot 2 \\  & =-4 \\  & \ne 0.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, since the Jacobian determinant is not zero, our system is $\text{almost linear}$ at ${x}^{∗}.$

EXPLANATION

The system can be rewritten in matrix form as x′=f(x) where x=[x(t)y(t)] and f(x)=[y2+cos⁡(πx)x2+cos⁡(πy)].

We need to compute the Jacobian determinant of f(x).

In our case, we have the following:

J=|∂f1∂x∂f1∂y∂f2∂x∂f2∂y|

First, we compute the partial derivatives:

∂f1∂x=∂∂x(y2+cos⁡(πx))=−πsin⁡(πx),∂f1∂y=∂∂y(y2+cos⁡(πx))=2y∂f2∂x=∂∂x(x2+cos⁡(πy))=2x,∂f2∂y=∂∂y(x2+cos⁡(πy))=−πsin⁡(πy)

Thus, we have

J=|−πsin⁡(πx)2y2x−πsin⁡(πy)|.

Next, we evaluate the Jacobian at the equilibrium x∗=[11] to get

J(1,1)=|−πsin⁡(π(1))2(1)2(1)−πsin⁡(π(1))|=|0220|=0⋅0−2⋅2=−4≠0.

Finally, since the Jacobian determinant is not zero, our system is almost linear at x∗.

content.worked_solution:
The system can be rewritten in matrix form as 

$$
{x}^{′}=\text{\boldsymbol}f(x)
$$

where $x=[\begin{aligned}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{aligned}]$ and 
$\text{\boldsymbol}f(x)=[\begin{aligned}{y}^{2}+\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi x) \\ {x}^{2}+\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi y)\end{aligned}].$

We need to compute the Jacobian determinant of $\text{\boldsymbol}f(x).$ 

In our case, we have the following:

$$
J=|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂x} & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂y} \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂x} & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂y}\end{aligned}|
$$

First, we compute the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({y}^{2}+\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi x))=-\pi \operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi x),\, & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({y}^{2}+\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi x))=2y \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}+\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi y))=2x,\, & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}+\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi y))=-\pi \operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi y)\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, we have

$$
J=|\begin{aligned}-\pi \operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi x) & 2y \\ 2x & -\pi \operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi y)\end{aligned}|.
$$

Next, we evaluate the Jacobian at the equilibrium ${x}^{∗}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]$ to get

$$
\begin{aligned}J(1,1) & =|\begin{aligned}-\pi \operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi (1)) & 2(1) \\ 2(1) & -\pi \operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi (1))\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}0 & 2 \\ 2 & 0\end{aligned}| \\  & =0\cdot 0-2\cdot 2 \\  & =-4 \\  & \ne 0.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, since the Jacobian determinant is not zero, our system is $\text{almost linear}$ at ${x}^{∗}.$

after.name: Question 3
after.problem:
$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t)={x}^{2}(t)+{y}^{2}(t) \\ {y}^{′}(t)={x}^{2}(t)-{y}^{2}(t)\end{aligned}
$$

Given the system of differential equations, select the correct options below.The Jacobian determinant of the system at the equilibrium point ${x}^{∗}=[0,\text{ }0]^{T}$ is given as

$$
J(0,0)={{field-1}}.
$$

At this point, the system is 
{{field-2}}
at ${x}^{∗}.$
after.worked_solution:
The system can be rewritten in matrix form as 

$$
{x}^{′}=f(x)
$$

where $x=[\begin{aligned}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{aligned}]$ and 
$f(x)=[\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+{y}^{2} \\ {x}^{2}-{y}^{2}\end{aligned}].$

We need to compute the Jacobian determinant of $f(x).$ 

In our case, we have the following:

$$
J=|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂x} & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂y} \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂x} & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂y}\end{aligned}|
$$

First, we compute the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})=2x,\, & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})=2y \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}-{y}^{2})=2x,\, & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}-{y}^{2})=-2y\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, we have

$$
J=|\begin{aligned}2x & 2y \\ 2x & -2y\end{aligned}|.
$$

Next, we evaluate the Jacobian at the equilibrium ${x}^{∗}=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0\end{aligned}]$ to get

$$
\begin{aligned}J(0,0) & =|\begin{aligned}2(0) & 2(0) \\ 2(0) & -2(0)\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}| \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, since the Jacobian determinant is zero, our system is $\text{not almost linear}$ at ${x}^{∗}.$

EXPLANATION

The system can be rewritten in matrix form as x′=f(x) where x=[x(t)y(t)] and f(x)=[x2+y2x2−y2].

We need to compute the Jacobian determinant of f(x).

In our case, we have the following:

J=|∂f1∂x∂f1∂y∂f2∂x∂f2∂y|

First, we compute the partial derivatives:

∂f1∂x=∂∂x(x2+y2)=2x,∂f1∂y=∂∂y(x2+y2)=2y∂f2∂x=∂∂x(x2−y2)=2x,∂f2∂y=∂∂y(x2−y2)=−2y

Thus, we have

J=|2x2y2x−2y|.

Next, we evaluate the Jacobian at the equilibrium x∗=[00] to get

J(0,0)=|2(0)2(0)2(0)−2(0)|=|0000|=0.

Finally, since the Jacobian determinant is zero, our system is not almost linear at x∗.

content.worked_solution:
The system can be rewritten in matrix form as 

$$
{x}^{′}=\text{\boldsymbol}f(x)
$$

where $x=[\begin{aligned}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{aligned}]$ and 
$\text{\boldsymbol}f(x)=[\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+{y}^{2} \\ {x}^{2}-{y}^{2}\end{aligned}].$

We need to compute the Jacobian determinant of $\text{\boldsymbol}f(x).$ 

In our case, we have the following:

$$
J=|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂x} & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂y} \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂x} & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂y}\end{aligned}|
$$

First, we compute the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})=2x,\, & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})=2y \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}-{y}^{2})=2x,\, & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}-{y}^{2})=-2y\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, we have

$$
J=|\begin{aligned}2x & 2y \\ 2x & -2y\end{aligned}|.
$$

Next, we evaluate the Jacobian at the equilibrium ${x}^{∗}=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0\end{aligned}]$ to get

$$
\begin{aligned}J(0,0) & =|\begin{aligned}2(0) & 2(0) \\ 2(0) & -2(0)\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}| \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, since the Jacobian determinant is zero, our system is $\text{not almost linear}$ at ${x}^{∗}.$

after.name: Question 4
after.problem:
$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t)=x(t)\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi y(t)) \\ {y}^{′}(t)=y(t)\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi x(t))\end{aligned}
$$

Given the system of differential equations, select the correct options below.The Jacobian determinant of the system at the equilibrium point ${x}^{∗}=[0,\text{ }1]^{T}$ is given as

$$
J(0,1)={{field-1}}.
$$

At this point, the system is 
{{field-2}}
at ${x}^{∗}.$
after.worked_solution:
The system can be rewritten in matrix form as 

$$
{x}^{′}=f(x)
$$

where $x=[\begin{aligned}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{aligned}]$ and 
$f(x)=[\begin{aligned}x\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi y) \\ y\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi x)\end{aligned}].$

We need to compute the Jacobian determinant of $f(x).$ 

In our case, we have the following:

$$
J=|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂x} & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂y} \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂x} & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂y}\end{aligned}|
$$

First, we compute the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(x\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi y))=\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi y),\, & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(x\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi y))=-\pi x\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi y) \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(y\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi x))=y\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi x),\, & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(y\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi x))=\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi x)\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, we have

$$
J=|\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi y) & -\pi x\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi y) \\ \pi y\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi x) & \operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi x)\end{aligned}|.
$$

Next, we evaluate the Jacobian at the equilibrium ${x}^{∗}=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]$ to get

$$
\begin{aligned}J(0,1) & =|\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi (1)) & -\pi (0)\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi (1)) \\ \pi (1)\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi (0)) & \operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi (0))\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}-1 & 0 \\ \pi  & 0\end{aligned}| \\  & =(-1)\cdot 0-0\cdot \pi  \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, since the Jacobian determinant is zero, our system is $\text{not almost linear}$ at ${x}^{∗}.$

EXPLANATION

The system can be rewritten in matrix form as x′=f(x) where x=[x(t)y(t)] and f(x)=[xcos⁡(πy)ysin⁡(πx)].

We need to compute the Jacobian determinant of f(x).

In our case, we have the following:

J=|∂f1∂x∂f1∂y∂f2∂x∂f2∂y|

First, we compute the partial derivatives:

∂f1∂x=∂∂x(xcos⁡(πy))=cos⁡(πy),∂f1∂y=∂∂y(xcos⁡(πy))=−πxsin⁡(πy)∂f2∂x=∂∂x(ysin⁡(πx))=ycos⁡(πx),∂f2∂y=∂∂y(ysin⁡(πx))=sin⁡(πx)

Thus, we have

J=|cos⁡(πy)−πxsin⁡(πy)πycos⁡(πx)sin⁡(πx)|.

Next, we evaluate the Jacobian at the equilibrium x∗=[01] to get

J(0,1)=|cos⁡(π(1))−π(0)sin⁡(π(1))π(1)cos⁡(π(0))sin⁡(π(0))|=|−10π0|=(−1)⋅0−0⋅π=0.

Finally, since the Jacobian determinant is zero, our system is not almost linear at x∗.

content.worked_solution:
The system can be rewritten in matrix form as 

$$
{x}^{′}=\text{\boldsymbol}f(x)
$$

where $x=[\begin{aligned}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{aligned}]$ and 
$\text{\boldsymbol}f(x)=[\begin{aligned}x\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi y) \\ y\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi x)\end{aligned}].$

We need to compute the Jacobian determinant of $\text{\boldsymbol}f(x).$ 

In our case, we have the following:

$$
J=|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂x} & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂y} \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂x} & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂y}\end{aligned}|
$$

First, we compute the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(x\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi y))=\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi y),\, & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(x\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi y))=-\pi x\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi y) \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(y\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi x))=y\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi x),\, & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(y\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi x))=\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi x)\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, we have

$$
J=|\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi y) & -\pi x\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi y) \\ \pi y\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi x) & \operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi x)\end{aligned}|.
$$

Next, we evaluate the Jacobian at the equilibrium ${x}^{∗}=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]$ to get

$$
\begin{aligned}J(0,1) & =|\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi (1)) & -\pi (0)\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi (1)) \\ \pi (1)\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi (0)) & \operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi (0))\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}-1 & 0 \\ \pi  & 0\end{aligned}| \\  & =(-1)\cdot 0-0\cdot \pi  \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, since the Jacobian determinant is zero, our system is $\text{not almost linear}$ at ${x}^{∗}.$

decision.explanation: The Jacobian matrix is [[2x, −π sin(πy)], [−π sin(πx), 2y]]. At (1,1), it is [[2,0],[0,2]], whose determinant is 4 ≠ 0. Thus the system is almost linear at this equilibrium.

after.name: Question 5
after.problem:
$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t)={x}^{2}(t)+\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi y(t)) \\ {y}^{′}(t)={y}^{2}(t)+\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi x(t))\end{aligned}
$$

Given the system of differential equations, select the correct options below.The Jacobian determinant of the system at the equilibrium point ${x}^{∗}=[1,\text{ }1]^{T}$ is given as

$$
J(1,1)={{field-1}}.
$$

At this point, the system is 
{{field-2}}
at ${x}^{∗}.$
after.worked_solution:
The system can be rewritten in matrix form as 

$$
{x}^{′}=f(x)
$$

where $x=[\begin{aligned}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{aligned}]$ and 
$f(x)=[\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi y) \\ {y}^{2}+\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi x)\end{aligned}].$

We need to compute the Jacobian determinant of $f(x).$ 

In our case, we have the following:

$$
J=|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂x} & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂y} \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂x} & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂y}\end{aligned}|
$$

First, we compute the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}+\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi y))=2x,\, & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}+\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi y))=-\pi \operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi y) \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({y}^{2}+\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi x))=-\pi \operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi x),\, & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({y}^{2}+\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi x))=2y\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, we have

$$
J=|\begin{aligned}2x & -\pi \operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi y) \\ -\pi \operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi x) & 2y\end{aligned}|.
$$

Next, we evaluate the Jacobian at the equilibrium ${x}^{∗}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]$ to get

$$
\begin{aligned}J(1,1) & =|\begin{aligned}2(1) & -\pi \operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi (1)) \\ -\pi \operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi (1)) & 2(1)\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}| \\  & =2\cdot 2-0\cdot 0 \\  & =4 \\  & \ne 0.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, since the Jacobian determinant is not zero, our system is $\text{almost linear}$ at ${x}^{∗}.$

EXPLANATION

The system can be rewritten in matrix form as x′=f(x) where x=[x(t)y(t)] and f(x)=[x2+cos⁡(πy)y2+cos⁡(πx)].

We need to compute the Jacobian determinant of f(x).

In our case, we have the following:

J=|∂f1∂x∂f1∂y∂f2∂x∂f2∂y|

First, we compute the partial derivatives:

∂f1∂x=∂∂x(x2+cos⁡(πy))=2x,∂f1∂y=∂∂y(x2+cos⁡(πy))=−πsin⁡(πy)∂f2∂x=∂∂x(y2+cos⁡(πx))=−πsin⁡(πx),∂f2∂y=∂∂y(y2+cos⁡(πx))=2y

Thus, we have

J=|2x−πsin⁡(πy)−πsin⁡(πx)2y|.

Next, we evaluate the Jacobian at the equilibrium x∗=[11] to get

J(1,1)=|2(1)−πsin⁡(π(1))−πsin⁡(π(1))2(1)|=|2002|=2⋅2−0⋅0=4≠0.

Finally, since the Jacobian determinant is not zero, our system is almost linear at x∗.

content.worked_solution:
The system can be rewritten in matrix form as 

$$
{x}^{′}=\text{\boldsymbol}f(x)
$$

where $x=[\begin{aligned}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{aligned}]$ and 
$\text{\boldsymbol}f(x)=[\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi y) \\ {y}^{2}+\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi x)\end{aligned}].$

We need to compute the Jacobian determinant of $\text{\boldsymbol}f(x).$ 

In our case, we have the following:

$$
J=|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂x} & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂y} \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂x} & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂y}\end{aligned}|
$$

First, we compute the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}+\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi y))=2x,\, & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}+\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi y))=-\pi \operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi y) \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({y}^{2}+\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi x))=-\pi \operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi x),\, & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({y}^{2}+\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi x))=2y\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, we have

$$
J=|\begin{aligned}2x & -\pi \operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi y) \\ -\pi \operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi x) & 2y\end{aligned}|.
$$

Next, we evaluate the Jacobian at the equilibrium ${x}^{∗}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]$ to get

$$
\begin{aligned}J(1,1) & =|\begin{aligned}2(1) & -\pi \operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi (1)) \\ -\pi \operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi (1)) & 2(1)\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}| \\  & =2\cdot 2-0\cdot 0 \\  & =4 \\  & \ne 0.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, since the Jacobian determinant is not zero, our system is $\text{almost linear}$ at ${x}^{∗}.$

after.worked_solution:
The system can be rewritten in matrix form as 

$$
{x}^{′}=f(x)
$$

where $x=[\begin{aligned}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{aligned}]$ and 
$f(x)=[\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+xy-2x+3y+5 \\ {y}^{2}-x+4y+4\end{aligned}].$

We need to compute the Jacobian matrix (or the total derivative) of $f(x).$ 

In our case, we have the following:

$$
{f}^{′}(x)=[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂x} & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂y} \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂x} & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂y}\end{aligned}]
$$

First, we compute the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}+xy-2x+3y+5)=2x+y-2,\, & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}+xy-2x+3y+5)=x+3 \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({y}^{2}-x+4y+4)=-1,\, & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({y}^{2}-x+4y+4)=2y+4\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, we have

$$
{f}^{′}(x)=[\begin{aligned}2x+y-2 & x+3 \\ -1 & 2y+4\end{aligned}].
$$

Next, we evaluate the Jacobian at the equilibrium ${x}^{∗}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1\end{aligned}]$ to get

$$
{f}^{′}({x}^{∗})=[\begin{aligned}2(1)+(-1)-2 & 1+3 \\ -1 & 2(-1)+4\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 4 \\ -1 & 2\end{aligned}].
$$

Finally, near the equilibrium, the nonlinear system is approximated by

$$
{u}^{′}=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 4 \\ -1 & 2\end{aligned}]u,
$$

where the deviation vector is

$$
u=x-{x}^{∗}=[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}x-1 \\ y+1\end{aligned}].
$$

$$
{x}^{′}=\text{\boldsymbol}f(x)
$$

where $x=[\begin{aligned}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{aligned}]$ and 
$\text{\boldsymbol}f(x)=[\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+xy-2x+3y+5 \\ {y}^{2}-x+4y+4\end{aligned}].$

We need to compute the Jacobian matrix (or the total derivative) of $\text{\boldsymbol}f(x).$ 

In our case, we have the following:

$$
\text{\boldsymbol}{f}^{′}(x)=[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂x} & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂y} \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂x} & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂y}\end{aligned}]

$$

after.worked_solution:
The system can be rewritten in matrix form as 

$$
{x}^{′}=f(x)
$$

where $x=[\begin{aligned}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{aligned}]$ and 
$f(x)=[\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+x \\ 2x+3y\end{aligned}].$

We need to compute the Jacobian matrix (or the total derivative) of $f(x).$ 

In our case, we have the following:

$$
{f}^{′}(x)=[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂x} & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂y} \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂x} & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂y}\end{aligned}]
$$

First, we compute the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+x)=2x+1,\, & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+x)=2y \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(2x+3y)=2,\, & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(2x+3y)=3\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, we have

$$
{f}^{′}(x)=[\begin{aligned}2x+1 & 2y \\ 2 & 3\end{aligned}].
$$

Now evaluate the Jacobian at the equilibrium at ${x}^{∗}=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0\end{aligned}]$ to get 

$$
{f}^{′}({x}^{∗})=[\begin{aligned}2(0)+1 & 2(0) \\ 2 & 3\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 2 & 3\end{aligned}].
$$

Notice that the matrix is invertible (its determinant is not zero), so the system is almost linear at ${x}^{∗}.$

To find the eigenvalue of the Jacobian matrix, we write down the characteristic equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}|\begin{aligned}1-\lambda  & 0 \\ 2 & 3-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (1-\lambda )(3-\lambda ) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Solving the equation, we get the eigenvalues ${\lambda }_{1,2}=1,\text{ }3.$

Finally, since we both have two real and positive eigenvalues, our equilibrium is an $\text{unstable}$ $\text{source}.$

|1−λ023−λ|=0(1−λ)(3−λ)=0

$$

$$

\text{\boldsymbol}{f}^{′}({x}^{∗})=[\begin{aligned}2(0)+1 & 2(0) \\ 2 & 3\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 2 & 3\end{aligned}].
$$

Notice that the matrix is invertible (its determinant is not zero), so the system is almost linear at ${x}^{∗}.$

To find the eigenvalue of the Jacobian matrix, we write down the characteristic equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}|\begin{aligned}1-\lambda  & 0 \\ 2 & 3-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (1-\lambda )(3-\lambda ) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Solving the equation, we get the eigenvalues ${\lambda }_{1,2}=1,\text{ }3.$

after.worked_solution:
The system can be rewritten in matrix form as 

$$
{x}^{′}=f(x)
$$

where $x=[\begin{aligned}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{aligned}]$ and 
$f(x)=[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi x)+y \\ 1-{x}^{2}\end{aligned}].$

We need to compute the Jacobian matrix (or the total derivative) of $f(x).$ 

In our case, we have the following:

$$
{f}^{′}(x)=[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂x} & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂y} \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂x} & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂y}\end{aligned}]
$$

First, we compute the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\frac{1}{\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi x)+y)=\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi x) \\ \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(\frac{1}{\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi x)+y)=1 \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(1-{x}^{2})=-2x \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(1-{x}^{2})=0\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, we have

$$
{f}^{′}(x)=[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi x) & 1 \\ -2x & 0\end{aligned}].
$$

Next, we evaluate the Jacobian at the equilibrium ${x}^{∗}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]$ to get

$$
{f}^{′}({x}^{∗})=[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi (1)) & 1 \\ -2(1) & 0\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 \\ -2 & 0\end{aligned}].
$$

Notice that the matrix is invertible (its determinant is not zero), so the system is almost linear at ${x}^{∗}.$

To find the eigenvalues of the Jacobian matrix, we write down the characteristic equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}|\begin{aligned}-1-\lambda  & 1 \\ -2 & -\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ -\lambda \cdot (-1-\lambda )-1\cdot (-2) & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}+\lambda +2 & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Solving the equation, we get the eigenvalues ${\lambda }_{1,2}=-\frac{1}{2}\pm \frac{\sqrt{7}}{2}\text{i}.$

Finally, since we have two complex eigenvalues with negative real parts, our equilibrium is an $\text{asymptotically stable}$ $\text{spiral sink}.$

\begin{aligned}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂x} & =2+3{x}^{2},\, & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂y} & =1 \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂x} & =-2,\, & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂y} & =3{y}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, we have

$$
{f}^{′}(x)=[\begin{aligned}2+3{x}^{2} & 1 \\ -2 & 3{y}^{2}\end{aligned}].
$$

Next, we evaluate the Jacobian at the equilibrium ${x}^{∗}=[0,\text{ }0]^{T}$ to get

$$
{f}^{′}({x}^{∗})=[\begin{aligned}2+0 & 1 \\ -2 & 0\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ -2 & 0\end{aligned}].
$$

To find the eigenvalues of the Jacobian matrix, we write down the characteristic equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}|\begin{aligned}2-\lambda  & 1 \\ -2 & -\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (2-\lambda )(-\lambda )+2 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}-2\lambda +2 & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Solving the equation, we get the eigenvalues ${\lambda }_{1,2}=1\pm i.$

Since we have two complex eigenvalues with positive real parts, our equilibrium is an $\text{unstable}$ $\text{spiral source}.$
